findings.finding: The first non-right-triangle calculation adds both an unsupplied perpendicular construction and two linked right-triangle calculations.
findings.breakdown: Students must create the right triangles and recognise their shared height before any taught ratio applies. Questions 5–7 require only one supplied right triangle.
findings.checked: p3-equilateral supplies its altitude. No preceding practice asks students to construct an altitude and carry a calculated length between two triangles. The later equilateral-height question p9-q11-b prepares only the construction, so moving it alone would not fully bridge the transition. The proposed cue gives a valid route: h=6 sin60°, then x=h/sin45°.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary right-triangle trigonometry and surd arithmetic are prior knowledge. Exact calculations here are without a calculator.

repair.proposal: Add to p7-q8-a: ‘Draw a perpendicular from the top vertex to the base and call its length h. Use the side of length 6 to find h, then use the other right triangle to find x.’ Keep parts b–d in their existing order.

findings.doneWhen: The first shared-height calculation supplies the construction and linking strategy while students still select ratios and calculate.

findings.finding: The named independent tasks repeat unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Later copies require the same response from the same givens and support. They add no mathematical variation.
findings.checked: Compared the complete targeted stems, parts, values and diagram provision. The exact-value memorisation instruction does not specify a retrieval schedule or explain these exact repetitions. Supported-to-independent repetitions have different whole tasks and are excluded. The quadrant comparison in p39-q4 is retained.
findings.assumptions: Each independently answerable part is a whole task. No additional repetition purpose is supplied.

repair.proposal: Keep the first copy of each matched task. Remove p5-q2-g, p5-q2-h, p5-q2-i, p5-q2-j, p5-q2-k, p5-q2-l, p5-q2-m, p5-q2-n, p5-q2-o and p5-q2-p; remove p5-q3-j, p5-q3-k, p5-q3-l, p5-q3-m, p5-q3-n, p5-q3-o and p5-q3-p; remove the unchanged independent parts p6-q4-a through p6-q4-x and p6-q4-q-repeat, p6-q4-r-repeat, p6-q4-s-repeat and p6-q4-t-repeat. Remove p18-q1-c, p18-q1-h, p18-q1-n and p18-q1-o; p25-q1-e, p25-q1-o, p25-q1-n and p25-q1-u; p29-q1-q; p33-q2-d; p38-q3-f; p39-q5-c; and p40-q9-i, p40-q9-c, p40-q9-a, p40-q9-b, p40-q9-j, p40-q9-n and p40-q9-m. Preserve the complete quadrant runs in p39-q4 and all repetitions with changed scaffolds.

findings.doneWhen: Each targeted unchanged task appears once, with supported-to-independent practice and protected comparisons preserved.

findings.finding: Explain the complementary tangent product and identify when its factors are equal.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the supplied reciprocal identity into a general explanation using right-triangle side ratios.
findings.checked: For acute x, opposite and adjacent lengths are positive, so both tangent factors exist. Their product is 1. Equality implies equal legs and hence x=45°. The required methods are available by the end of this topic.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary right-triangle ratios and the angle sum of a triangle are prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: After p13-q5, add an optional task: ‘For an acute angle x, explain using opposite and adjacent sides why tan x × tan(90°−x)=1. When are the two factors equal? Explain using the triangle.’ Expected answer: the factors are a/c and c/a, so their product is 1. Equal factors require a²=c²; positive side lengths give a=c. The triangle is isosceles, x=45°, and both factors equal 1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks for the general explanation and correctly identifies the unique acute equal-factor case.

findings.finding: The bearing-conversion question introduces a change of both starting axis and rotation direction without modelling their reconciliation.
findings.breakdown: Students may reuse the bearing or apply 90°−bearing without obtaining the required positive inclination for bearings above 90°.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching defines inclination and contrasts correct and incorrect measurements, but never combines that convention with true bearings. Questions 1–2 use only inclinations. The proposed 120° example correctly gives 330°.
findings.assumptions: True bearings are prior knowledge from Elevation, Depression, Bearings. Conversion to this booklet's new inclination convention is not supplied there as evidence. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p16-q3, add: ‘True bearings are measured clockwise from north; inclinations are measured anticlockwise from east. Sketch the bearing direction, then measure anticlockwise from east. A bearing of 120° points 30° below east, so its inclination is 360°−30°=330°.’

findings.doneWhen: A preceding worked conversion explicitly reconciles the two axes and rotation directions and obtains a positive inclination.

findings.finding: Every supplied reduction demonstration needs only one adjustment, leaving the incorrect one-adjustment rule unexposed in worked teaching.
findings.breakdown: A student following the demonstrated shortcut can stop at 360°, 540° or −640° instead of checking whether the result is in the required range.
findings.checked: p17-information-rules-block explicitly says ‘repeatedly’, but under the stated special-case test a general rule alone does not expose the wrong shortcut. Both worked reductions finish after one adjustment; the multi-turn response questions have no supplied question-side intermediate check.
findings.assumptions: Practice worked answers are not preceding teaching. Calculator access is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before p17-rewrite-c, add: ‘720°−360°=360°. This is still outside 0°≤θ<360°, so subtract again: 360°−360°=0°. After every adjustment, check the range. For a negative angle, keep adding 360° while the result is below 0°.’

findings.doneWhen: Teaching models an intermediate range check and a second adjustment, explicitly excluding 360°.

findings.finding: The numerical rewriting examples omit the calculation connecting each given inclination to its reference angle.
findings.breakdown: The examples combine reference-angle selection with sign selection, but present 20° and 65° without writing the respective subtraction.
findings.checked: p23, p24 and p30 teach the reference-angle rules earlier. That establishes the method, but does not supply the connecting numerical step inside these examples. The standard explicitly requires that step when working substitutes a derived value.

repair.proposal: Write the first lines as A=200°−180°=20° and A=360°−295°=65°, respectively.

findings.doneWhen: Both examples explicitly show how their numerical reference angles come from their given inclinations.

findings.finding: Determine when reversing an angle preserves its sine or cosine.
findings.breakdown: The task connects negative rotations with the unit-circle coordinate definitions.
findings.checked: Reflection in the x-axis changes the sign of the sine coordinate and preserves the cosine coordinate. In 0°≤θ<360°, sine is unchanged only at 0° and 180°; cosine is unchanged throughout. Unit-circle coordinates and negative rotations are already taught.
findings.assumptions: Students can reason about reflected Cartesian coordinates.

repair.proposal: After p34-q7, add an optional task: ‘For 0°≤θ<360°, find all θ for which sin(−θ)=sinθ. Then determine when cos(−θ)=cosθ. Explain using the unit circle.’ Expected answer: sine agrees at θ=0° and 180° because reflection preserves the y-coordinate only when it is zero. Cosine agrees for every θ because the x-coordinate is unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: The task and expected answer distinguish the sine boundary cases from the unrestricted cosine relationship.

findings.finding: The tangent investigation asks students to show vertical asymptotes before explaining that graph feature.
findings.breakdown: Undefined table entries identify excluded angles, but do not explain dashed vertical lines or separate branches approaching them. Students may treat the exclusions as isolated missing points.
findings.checked: p3-endpoints discusses approaching 90° and division by zero, and p45 supplies the first rising branch. Neither introduces an asymptote or explains the branch on the other side. p45-property-5 names the feature after the graph task; the division-by-zero explanation alone does not describe nearby behaviour.
findings.assumptions: Teacher-led investigation can remain in place. A short introduction to the requested graph feature is sufficient.

repair.proposal: Before p45-graph-response, add: ‘As θ approaches 90° or 270°, tangent values become arbitrarily large in magnitude. The corresponding vertical lines are called asymptotes. Draw dashed lines at θ=90° and θ=270° and separate branches approaching them. Do not join the curve across these lines.’

findings.doneWhen: Students meet the meaning and drawing convention of vertical asymptotes before being asked to show them.

findings.finding: Vary the horizontal level to expose how the number of sine solutions changes at the maximum.
findings.breakdown: The run contrasts two intersections, one intersection and no intersection while holding the function and domain fixed.
findings.checked: The proposed counts are 2, 2, 1 and 0 on 0°≤θ<360°. The follow-up has two solutions, −180° and 180°, within its open domain. Graph intersection counting is taught in p47; no new solving method is needed.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p47-guided-d, add: ‘For 0°≤θ<360°, predict the number of solutions before drawing each horizontal line: (a) sinθ=0.5; (b) sinθ=0.9; (c) sinθ=1; (d) sinθ=1.1. What changes as the line reaches and passes the maximum?’ Expected counts: 2, 2, 1, 0. Only the target level varies; the sine graph and domain remain fixed. Follow with: ‘How many solutions does cosθ=−1 have for −360°<θ<360°?’ Expected answer: 2.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict and explain the change in intersection count, then apply the idea to an unpatterned cosine question.

findings.finding: The equations topic does not rehearse converting a reference angle into an inclination in the required quadrant.
findings.breakdown: Students can find the reference angle and select quadrants yet fail to produce the corresponding solutions. This conversion is a substantial direct step in the complete worked examples.
findings.checked: p30 and p31 teach all four conversions. The immediately preceding graphs exercise uses graph readings and comparisons rather than practising those conversions throughout. p52 rehearses inverse-function calculations and p53 rehearses signs, leaving this separate recall step unrehearsed. The proposed four items are correct and fit a short review.
findings.assumptions: A degree-mode calculator is available. The missing review concerns quadrant conversion, not a calculator operation.

repair.proposal: Before p51-investigation, add: ‘Find θ for each reference angle and quadrant. Write the calculation: (a) A=20°, Q1; (b) A=20°, Q2; (c) A=20°, Q3; (d) A=20°, Q4.’ Expected answers: 20°; 180°−20°=160°; 180°+20°=200°; 360°−20°=340°.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review briefly rehearses all four conversions before the complete equation-solving examples.

findings.finding: Connect the geometric triangle-count cases to numerical height thresholds.
findings.breakdown: Varying only the opposite side exposes both boundaries of the two-triangle interval.
findings.checked: For A=30° and b=10 cm, h=5 cm. The counts for a=4, 5, 7, 10 and 12 cm are respectively 0, 1, 2, 1 and 1. At a=b the second construction is degenerate. For the follow-up, 9 sin40°≈5.79<8<9, so two triangles exist. These conditions are supplied in p65-cases.
findings.assumptions: A degree-mode calculator is available for the unpatterned follow-up.

repair.proposal: After p65-cases and before p66-teaching-method, add: ‘For each triangle, A=30° and b=10 cm. Before calculating angles, predict how many triangles are possible and explain using the perpendicular height: (1) a=4 cm; (2) a=5 cm; (3) a=7 cm; (4) a=10 cm; (5) a=12 cm.’ Expected counts: 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, with height 5 cm. Only a varies; A and b remain fixed. Follow with: ‘How many triangles are possible when A=40°, b=9 cm and a=8 cm?’ Expected answer: two, since 9 sin40°≈5.79<8<9.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict and explain both threshold cases, then apply the conditions to an unpatterned example.
